name: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain

diagnosisContested.note: RCRSP is an umbrella label covering subacromial pain or impingement, rotator cuff tendinopathy, and partial-thickness and atraumatic full-thickness tears. Lewis (2016, narrative masterclass) reports that the extent to which a definitive structural diagnosis is achievable has been contested and lists the cause and source of symptoms and establishing a definitive diagnosis as unresolved. Guidelines still use the narrower terms 'rotator cuff tendinopathy' (JOSPT 2025) and 'subacromial pain' (Rees 2021).

avoidOrModify.movement: Resistance exercise whose load produces pain above 5/10 during the set, or leaves a pain increase that has not returned to the pre-exercise level by the next session
avoidOrModify.rationale: The Holmgren trial reduced load under this pain-monitoring rule, while allowing some pain during loading. RoCTEx used a similar rule: pain must not exceed 5/10, should not stay elevated more than 30 minutes after the workout, and should not worsen in the following days. SExSI reduced load if a flare lasted more than 24 hours. These are protocol rules, not tested thresholds: a scoping review found limits vary and most trials mention none. Painful and nonpainful exercise did not differ in Tran 2025 (very low to low certainty, not shoulder-specific) or Cavaggion 2024 (small RCT), so pain during a set may not need to be avoided. Cavaggion applied pain to one exercise only.

avoidOrModify.movement: Resisted band or equipment exercise performed quickly, under high loads and high repetitions, when the shoulder is easily aggravated with prolonged pain once provoked, together with night pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: Lewis states that this commonly aggravates the irritable presentation and advises load management (relative rest), aiming for an activity level that reduces pain. This is clinical opinion, not trial evidence.

avoidOrModify.movement: Starting with, or progressing to, higher-load or higher-volume resistance training on the assumption that it works better than lower load
avoidOrModify.rationale: This does not show harm. RoCTEx found no difference between progressive high load and low load (DASH adjusted difference -1.37, 95% CI -6.72 to 3.99). SExSI found no benefit from adding a large strengthening dose (SPADI MD 0.6, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.6) and no visible rise in flares (49 vs 47). JOSPT 2025 says high load cannot be recommended over low load (very low certainty). A dose review is conflicting, and a network meta-analysis said high-load training appeared to be the worst, from sparse data with implausible reported effects. The defensible position is not to assume heavier is better, not to treat heavy loading as dangerous.

avoidOrModify.movement: Daily, work or training activities that reliably provoke the shoulder pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: JOSPT 2025 recommends education including activity modification (Grade C, rec 24) and says ergonomic adaptations may be recommended (Grade C, rec 34). A Dutch guideline advises moving within the comfort zone and avoiding activities that are too long, heavy or frequent. Both GRASP arms included such advice, with no specific movements named. Its separate effect has not been isolated: no review abstract read tested activity modification as an intervention.

avoidOrModify.movement: Work tasks involving reaching, forward flexion or abduction above shoulder level
avoidOrModify.rationale: Only one guideline gives this advice: 'Limit movements such as reaching, forward flexion, and abduction above shoulder level'. It is a work recommendation aimed at preventing recurrence, and the guideline found no studies comparing preventive measures with none. Occupational reviews associate overhead work with cuff problems (OR 2.41; 2.23, 95% CI 1.98 to 2.52), but Diener concludes no reliable correlation can be established, and neither tested restricting overhead exercise. Acromiohumeral distance did not track pain, undercutting the impingement rationale. JOSPT 2025 and BESS 2025 do not restrict overhead exercise. This is not a ban; overhead exercise is a tolerance question.

Prefer the full-can (thumb-up) version. In 28 people with impingement, the empty can gave more pain (a 1-point difference, P=.003) and scapular positions reported to reduce subacromial space. A lab study in asymptomatic men, and another whose abstract does not state symptom status, also favour the full can on kinematics. The pain difference is small and acute, and no trial tested outcomes.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lateral raises and upright rows taken above 90 degrees
avoidOrModify.rationale: In 77 men, clinical impingement signs among weight trainers were associated with these exercises above 90 degrees (p<=0.004), and inversely associated with external rotator strengthening. This is a cross-sectional association in men, with no imaging, so cause is unknown. Keeping the range lower while symptomatic is a reasonable modification, not a proven one.

avoidOrModify.movement: Behind-the-neck press and pulldown; the full 'high-five' end position in overhead pressing
avoidOrModify.rationale: An integrative review advises against behind-the-neck variants and suggests raising the arms slightly in front of the head without full extension, drawn largely from narrative and cross-sectional sources. EMG studies in healthy lifters measure muscle activity only and do not show safety either way. No trial tested this in people with shoulder pain.

avoidOrModify.movement: Bench press with a narrow (1 bi-acromial width) grip or elbows at 45 degrees of abduction
avoidOrModify.rationale: A modelling study estimated raised superior shear with these setups, and its authors say that for subacromial pain it might be better to avoid them. Grip below 1.5 bi-acromial widths and scapular retraction lowered other estimated loads. Abduction mattered less overall than grip and scapula position. The participants were ten healthy athletes, the reported comparisons used a 16 kg bar and forces were estimated, so injury causation is not shown.

candidateExercises.name: Eccentric-emphasis rotator cuff strengthening with band or light weight

dose.frequency: Trial dose: twice daily for 8 weeks, then once daily for 4 weeks

candidateExercises.cautions: The trial appendix shows a full-can raise for supraspinatus and side-lying external rotation for infraspinatus and teres minor, with weeks 9 to 12 becoming concentric/eccentric (3 sets of 10, then 15, repetitions). The article says load came from weights and elastic bands. Participants had pain for more than 6 months, were on an orthopaedic pathway, received a corticosteroid injection first, and had physiotherapist-adjusted load. Do not treat this high-frequency dose as a proven unsupervised minimum. Certainty for eccentric programmes over nonspecific exercise is low to very low. Later evidence does not favour eccentric work: JOSPT 2025 reports one analysis with no significant pain or disability benefit over other exercise and another with a medium-term pain benefit only (SMD -0.62, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.13, low certainty), Larsson 2019 found a pain difference it judged not clinically important, and Dejaco 2017 and Karabay 2025 found no added effect on pain or function. Larsson also reports 6 to 8 weeks as almost as effective as 12.

candidateExercises.name: Posterior shoulder stretch (cross-body)

dose.frequency: Trial dose: twice daily; holds were 30 to 60 seconds in the article and 30 to 45 in its appendix, 30 is the lower bound

candidateExercises.cautions: The trial appendix photo shows a cross-body stretch with the back against a wall. It was one part of a multi-exercise programme and was not tested alone. RoCTEx used a shorter dose for its posterior capsule stretch: five repetitions of 20 seconds in the protocol, three holds of about 15 seconds in the published appendix. A meta-analysis of modified posterior stretching reports large effects (activity pain SMD -1.45, 95% CI -2.49 to -0.41) from small trials, with no GRADE rating and no dose in the abstract. Cooper 2023 suggests flexibility work may beat resistance at the shoulder, on low-quality evidence.

candidateExercises.name: Arm-supported isometric hold in the direction of pain

dose.frequency: No dose found in the sources opened

candidateExercises.cautions: Lewis calls this anecdotal and says conclusive evidence for the shoulder is not available. Individual response should decide whether it continues. A review found limited evidence that isometrics are not superior to isotonic exercise for chronic tendinopathy, and for acute rotator cuff tendinopathy no more effective than ice in the short term. Only 2 of its studies were in the rotator cuff, and 7 of 10 were of poor quality.

candidateExercises.name: Short-lever shoulder flexion, or flexion supported on a ball

dose.frequency: No dose found in the sources opened

candidateExercises.cautions: Offered by Lewis as gentle loading for the irritable presentation; it should ideally not increase pain. Progress only as tolerated. A meta-analysis favours motor control programmes slightly, but it cannot separate their effect from progression and tailoring, and did not test this specific exercise.

candidateExercises.name: Lower-load rotator cuff strengthening (RoCTEx low-load arm)

dose.frequency: Trial dose: 3 times per week for 12 weeks; 20 to 25 repetitions (20 is the lower bound), about 30 seconds rest

candidateExercises.cautions: No significant difference from high load in this trial, with compliance of only 57% to 61%. Six-exercise home programme in the protocol: push-up plus, low row, scaption, side-lying external rotation, posterior capsule stretch, scapulae retraction, with scapular exercises at 20 RM. Pain must not exceed 5/10, or stay elevated beyond 30 minutes, or increase in following days. The trial excluded resting pain over 40 mm VAS, under 90 degrees of active elevation, full-thickness rupture, frozen shoulder and labral lesions.

candidateExercises.name: Progressive high-load rotator cuff strengthening (RoCTEx high-load arm)

dose.frequency: Trial dose: 3 times per week for 12 weeks; repetitions step down from 15 in week 1, 12 in weeks 2-3, 10 in weeks 4-5, 8 in weeks 6-8, to 6 in weeks 9-12 (15 RM to 6 RM); about 30 seconds rest, about 3 to 4 seconds on each lifting and lowering phase of the rotator cuff exercises

candidateExercises.cautions: Not better than low load overall (DASH adjusted difference -1.37, 95% CI -6.72 to 3.99). A small subgroup interaction favoured high load with concomitant corticosteroid. Three patients across the trial were referred for operation for worsening (2 high-load, 1 low-load). At least one episode of increased pain over 1 hour affected 30.2% of high-load and 36.7% of low-load patients, with no significant difference. Same pain rule and exclusions as the low-load arm. Physiotherapy sessions supported progression.

candidateExercises.name: Banded external rotation in about 45 degrees of scaption and abduction to about 45 degrees, with an isometric pause (SExSI add-on)

dose.frequency: Trial dose: 3 phases of 5 to 6 weeks, adding 1 exercise and load per phase, to contraction failure; phase 1 was 15 to 20 repetition maximum (15 is the lower bound) with slow contractions and a 5-second isometric component. Sets and weekly frequency are not stated in the main article

candidateExercises.cautions: Null trial: adding this to usual care gave no benefit at 4 months (SPADI MD 0.6, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.6), so authors say adding more exercise is not a viable solution. Adherence was about a quarter of prescribed time under tension. Reduce load if a flare lasts more than 24 hours. Exercises: external rotation with elbow supported, abduction to about 45 degrees, external rotation with elbow unsupported.

candidateExercises.name: Resisted external rotation, flexion and abduction with bands (GRASP progressive programme)

dose.frequency: Trial dose: 5 days per week with 2 non-consecutive recovery days, over 16 weeks, with up to 6 supervised sessions. Sets and repetitions are not in the main paper or its protocol, which individualises volume and load using the modified Borg scale

candidateExercises.cautions: No better than one advice session with self-guided exercise over 12 months (SPADI MD -0.66, 99% CI -4.52 to 3.20). No serious adverse events; minor flares were not captured. Home programme, not gym lifting.

candidateExercises.name: Self-paced progressive shoulder programme to moderate effort

dose.frequency: Cohort dose: at least 4 times per week for 12 weeks; repetitions as many as possible with good technique, without sharp pain, to fatigue; modified Borg effort 4 to 6 out of 10

candidateExercises.cautions: Uncontrolled cohort of 143 people, so effects cannot be attributed to the programme. Pain advice was to work 'to but not through' pain. The extract did not name each exercise.

candidateExercises.name: Assisted range of motion (pulley or assisted abduction, elevation, rotation), then banded and scapular work

dose.frequency: Consensus dose: weeks 0 to 6, high-repetition movement four times every day; weeks 6 to 12, strength and control work at least once a day. No repetition counts given

candidateExercises.cautions: Expert consensus only (level 2 or lower), from a regional panel with no patients. The only staged dose found. Pavlova 2023 reports larger pooled effects with less-than-daily resistance loading, so high frequency is not established, and no adverse-event data come with this dose.

redFlags.sign: Shoulder dislocation after trauma that has not been put back in place

redFlags.action: Stop exercising and see a clinician promptly. The source specifies urgent referral on the local two-week cancer pathway.

redFlags.sign: Suspected acute rotator cuff tear after a traumatic event
redFlags.action: Stop exercising. Urgent referral, ideally the next available outpatient clinic. Consensus timing: acute traumatic tears with dramatic loss of function should see a surgeon within 6 weeks, and large acute tears of 2 or more tendons (over 3 cm) within 4 weeks. Trial results may not apply to traumatic tears, large tears involving subscapularis, or young people.

redFlags.sign: New inflammatory arthritis with symptoms of inflammation in several joints
redFlags.action: Urgent referral through local rheumatology pathways.

redFlags.sign: Shoulder symptoms that may be referred from elsewhere, such as the neck, chest or abdomen, nerves or blood vessels
redFlags.action: Do not attribute them to the rotator cuff. Stop and get medical assessment; urgency depends on the symptoms.

redFlags.sign: Shoulder pain in a child or adolescent
redFlags.action: Do not use this adult guidance. Urgent medical referral, as the source specifies for this group.

redFlags.sign: Severe or persistent pain or disability that has not improved after 12 weeks of non-surgical care
redFlags.action: Not an emergency. See a clinician for reassessment or specialist referral. The source grades this F (expert opinion).

valuesCorrected: RoCTEx high-load tempo: about 2 seconds on lowering corrected to about 3 to 4 seconds on each lifting and lowering phase of the rotator cuff exercises (Appendix B).
RoCTEx adverse events: the unassigned 30% to 37% corrected to 30.2% high-load and 36.7% low-load (Table 1).
RoCTEx referrals: three patients attributed to the high-load caution corrected to 2 high-load and 1 low-load.
RoCTEx stretch: the published appendix gives three holds of about 15 seconds, while the protocol gives five of 20 seconds. Both are now recorded.
JOSPT 2025 eccentric evidence: 'no significant benefit' corrected, because one of its two analyses reports medium-term pain SMD -0.62 (-1.11 to -0.13, low certainty).
Wu 2025: 'no clear superiority over general exercise' corrected. It reports modest effects favouring specific over non-specific exercise.
Cavaggion 2024: 14% vs 5% is the share with 4 to 7 episodes of persistent pain or fatigue, not the share with any episode.
JOSPT 2025 rec 36 concerns patient-rated outcome tools, not capacity and load tolerance, which is rec 35.
Gundersen 2026: 'healthy' corrected to 'resistance-trained', as the abstract states.
SExSI exercise name: abduction was to about 45 degrees with slight scaption, not abduction in 45 degrees of scaption.
Empty-can item: 'lab studies in people without symptoms' corrected. Only Robert-Lachaine states asymptomatic participants in its abstract.
Pain rule: 'need not be avoided outright' corrected to Tran 2025's 'may not need to be avoided', and Cavaggion's one-exercise contrast added.
Holmgren weeks 9 to 12: 3 sets of 10, then 15, repetitions added from the appendix.
Noteboom: the 16 kg bar used in the reported comparisons added.
GRASP dose: the protocol was opened. It gives no sets or repetitions and uses the modified Borg scale, so it is now cited.
Access levels: Rees 2021, Wu 2025, Lewis 2016 and the GRASP protocol changed from not_reconfirmed to full_text after being opened.
unverifiable: Publisher landing pages return HTTP 403 to automated requests, and Thieme (Diener 2024, Pirruccio 2019) returned 404 to them. DOI redirects go to the expected publisher, and all 83 PMIDs, DOIs and PMCIDs agree in PubMed. BESS and AAOS have no PMID and were checked from their PDFs. The Thieme DOIs were confirmed through PubMed metadata only.

Depth: all sources were checked at abstract or metadata level. Full text was read by keyword only for sources behind avoidOrModify items, doses and red flags, plus Rees 2021 by section. The other evidence-summary claims were checked against abstracts, so details not in an abstract were not confirmed.
Holmgren appendix photos were not re-examined; only its text was read. The cross-body wall stretch and catalog match therefore rest on the earlier pass.
Page 2016 dose details (10 sessions, 22 weeks) were not reopened; the Cochrane full text was not retrieved in this pass. The abstract numbers were confirmed.
Zhang W 2025: no numeric SUCRA for high-load training was readable, as ranking figures are images.
Thigpen 2006: symptom status is not stated in the abstract and the full text is paywalled.
PASE clinical results were not searched for again in this pass.

limitations: Grade stays low for specific exercise guidance, although guidelines strongly endorse exercise: JOSPT 2025 gives Grade A and BESS 2025 a strong positive, but on evidence that is often low or very low in certainty, with optimal parameters stated as unknown. Nothing found tests overhead or pressing exercise as a treatment or restriction variable in rotator cuff pain: JOSPT 2025 mentions 'overhead' only in reference titles and BESS 2025 only as a diagnostic feature; the one overhead limit (Lambers Heerspink 2026) has no qualifying studies behind it. Press-specific evidence is biomechanical, EMG or cross-sectional, in mostly healthy lifters. CONTRADICTIONS. (1) Exercise benefit: Steuri 2017 (very low quality), Silveira 2024 and Pieters 2020 favour exercise; Page 2016, Liu 2026 and Dube 2023 report little or no important difference against placebo, passive care or education; Liu's very wide intervals do not prove equivalence. (2) Load: Zhang W 2025 says high load appeared worst, Malliaras 2020 conflicts, and RoCTEx and SExSI were null; Zhang's reported values such as 23.87 are implausible as SMDs and its direction conflicts with its own convention. (3) Eccentric emphasis: Diercks 2014 favours it; JOSPT 2025, BESS 2025, Lafrance 2024 and Larsson 2019 do not support superiority. Holmgren's programme included it, but its control was unloaded. (4) Pain rules: Diercks 2014 and Chepeha 2025 stay within pain or 'to but not through' it; Holmgren and RoCTEx allow up to 5/10; Tran 2025 and Cavaggion 2024 find no difference; PASE clinical results were not found. Smith 2017's small benefit from painful exercise is superseded by Tran 2025. (5) Supervision: JOSPT 2025 finds supervised not superior (MD -0.31/10, low certainty), BESS leaves it uncertain, AAOS agrees only for post-repair patients, but Swinton 2023 links supervision to larger pre-post effects and Gutierrez-Espinoza 2026 reports a 25.2-point Constant-Murley advantage, where the programmes also differed in specificity. Hernandez-Sanchez 2025 prints CIs excluding zero with non-significant P values, so its figures should not be quoted as between-group effects. (6) Frequency: Holmgren used twice daily and Eubank four times daily, yet Pavlova 2023 reports larger pooled effects below daily, uncontrolled and across tendinopathies. (7) Modality: Cooper 2023 suggests flexibility may beat resistance at the shoulder, and its proprioception interval (lower bound -1.8) looks like a source typo. Zhang B 2026 finds strength gains only with exercise, within-group. (8) Subacromial space: Park 2020 and Cavaggion 2025 find it does not track symptoms, while Taghizadeh Delkhoush 2026, Noteboom 2024, Motlagh 2026 and Montoya-Minano 2026 reason from space or imaging; those are surrogate outcomes. Montoya-Minano's OR 17.7 rests on 15 trainers with very wide CI and groups differing in age and sex. (9) BESS 2025 says decompression shows no benefit over sham yet that surgery could be considered after 6 months; Vandvik 2019 strongly recommends against decompression; Lambers Heerspink Part 2 notes a 2021 module did the same; Petersson 2025 reports satisfying decompression results in non-responders, in a non-randomised comparison. (10) AAOS 2025 reports that with physical therapy for full-thickness tears, tear size may progress over 5 to 10 years (over 5 mm in 59%), so tear-free tendinopathy trials do not transfer to known tears. ACCESS. NICE CKS returned HTTP 403 and was not read. WHO was not searched separately. The Cochrane Library site was not queried directly. Abstract-only sources may hide doses and harms. Page 2016, Zhang W 2025, Pavlova 2023, Eubank 2016 and Diercks 2014 were read only in part; Ingwersen 2017 and Bonilla 2022 by keyword; the Dutch guideline updates mostly through model-assisted extraction. JOSPT 2025 Grade F for screening non-shoulder causes, formerly attributed to a secondary summary, was not in the data read from the original, so the attribution was dropped. Leong 2019 CIs are garbled in PubMed text and are omitted. DOSES. No guideline gives sets or repetitions. The numeric doses come from single trial protocols, several of them null, or from consensus. Adherence was often poor (RoCTEx 57% to 61%; SExSI about a quarter of prescribed time under tension; 50% unsupervised in Cavaggion 2023), so prescribed doses overstate what was done. They may not transfer to unsupervised use. Holmgren's population had long-standing symptoms, a corticosteroid injection first and physiotherapist-adjusted load. No candidate exercise was confirmed as matching a catalog entry except the cross-body stretch. Network rankings rest on small arms, so no concentric-over-eccentric preference is recorded. Wu 2025 has no GRADE rating. Red flags use clinician referral wording and need plain-language review before display. Traumatic presentations, full-thickness tears being considered for surgery, instability, frozen shoulder and inflammatory arthritis fall outside the trial evidence. This is general information for working around a condition, not diagnosis or treatment.
